title: Domination polynomials with many peaks: counterexamples to the Alikhani–Peng conjecture and the minimum-degree scale for a central mode
shortTitle: Domination polynomials need not be unimodal
oneLine: Two explicit 317,440-vertex graphs have more dominating sets of sizes 160,080 and 160,560 than of size 160,320, disproving the Alikhani–Peng unimodality conjecture with an exact integer certificate; minimum degree log₂ n + log₂ log₂ n + 1 restores a single central peak.
abstract: A set of vertices of a graph dominates it when every vertex is in the set or next to it. Counting dominating sets by size gives the sequence d_0, d_1, …, d_n of coefficients of the domination polynomial, and in 2009 Alikhani and Peng conjectured that this sequence is always unimodal. The conjecture had been proved for many graph classes and for minimum degree at least 2 log₂ n, and was listed as open in 2026. This candidate shows that it is false: an explicit connected split graph and an explicit connected bipartite graph, each on 317,440 vertices, satisfy d_160080 > d_160320 < d_160560, and an integer-arithmetic certificate proves the three inequalities. The mechanism is phase coexistence: two large families of dominating sets have exactly the same number of members but different typical sizes, and every other dominating set is negligible. The same idea gives connected graphs with order √n / log n separated peaks, and graphs in which every most frequent size is at distance of order n from the average size, answering a question of Beaton and Brown; for the explicit split graph no size within distance 88 of the average 160323.03… is a most frequent size. Counterexamples persist at minimum degree (1/2 + o(1)) log₂ n. In the positive direction, Σ_v (deg v + 2) 2^(−deg v − 1) ≤ 1 forces unimodality with the maximum at ⌈n/2⌉, so minimum degree log₂ n + log₂ log₂ n + 1 suffices, and for a maximum exactly at the middle this is best possible up to an additive constant. A side consequence is that single-site Glauber dynamics on dominating sets can mix exponentially slowly. Limits: the explicit example is large and not minimised; the linear mode–average gap needs astronomically large graphs and has a constant of order 10⁻²⁵; the least minimum degree forcing unimodality lies between (1/2 + o(1)) log₂ n and log₂ n + log₂ log₂ n + 1; trees remain open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 1.1 (exact certificate, main): there is a connected split graph and a connected bipartite graph, each on 317,440 vertices, with d_160080 > d_160320 < d_160560; in units of 10⁻⁶ · 2^314880 the three coefficients lie in [1556, 1615], [1482, 1541] and [1565, 1624]. The Alikhani–Peng conjecture is false.
Theorem 1.2 (proof): along infinite sequences of orders n, connected split and bipartite graphs have at least c√n / log n peak regions; explicitly, four peak regions on 4,857,004,032 vertices.

Theorem 1.3 (proof and certificate): every global mode can be at distance of order n from the average size avd(G); for the explicit split graph 160323.034984 ≤ avd(G) ≤ 160323.034985 and no index in [160217, 160412] is a global mode. This answers a question of Beaton and Brown.

Theorem 1.4 (proof, main): nonunimodal graphs exist with δ(G)/log₂ n → 1/2; Σ_v (deg v + 2) 2^(−deg v − 1) ≤ 1 forces unimodality with a global mode at ⌈n/2⌉, so δ ≥ log₂ n + log₂ log₂ n + 1 suffices (n ≥ 4); for a mode exactly at ⌈n/2⌉ this is best possible up to an additive constant.
Proposition 6.3 (proof): single-site Glauber dynamics on dominating sets mixes in time e^{Ω(n)} on the graphs of Section 6.

narration:
This is an audio briefing from Evidence Press on a research candidate about counting the ways to cover a network.

A dominating set in a network is a set of nodes such that every node is either in the set or directly linked to one that is, like placing guards so that every site is watched. Count the dominating sets of each size and you get a sequence of numbers. In every network anyone had checked, this sequence climbs to a single peak and then falls. Alikhani and Peng conjectured that this always happens, and the question was still listed as open.

This candidate shows that the conjecture is false. It builds two explicit connected networks, each with 317,440 nodes. In both, there are more dominating sets of size 160,080 than of size 160,320, and more again of size 160,560 than of the middle size. So the count dips and then rises again, and an exact integer calculation proves all three comparisons.

The idea is to build two large families of dominating sets that have exactly the same number of members but different typical sizes, while every other dominating set is comparatively rare. The sizes then form two humps, and the count dips in between. The same idea gives networks with many separate peaks, and networks in which the most common size sits far from the average size, which answers a question of Beaton and Brown. In the other direction, if every node has a little more than the base-two logarithm of the number of nodes as its number of neighbours, the sequence does have a single peak, exactly at the middle.

The limits are clear: the example is large and has not been minimised, the exact degree threshold for a single peak is still open, and the question for trees remains open.

This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and exact computer arithmetic rather than by peer review, and this briefing uses a synthetic voice that is not additional evidence.

decisionObject.description: Know whether the domination polynomial of every graph is unimodal, how far its mode can sit from the average size, and which minimum degree forces a single central peak.
decisionObject.scope: Finite simple graphs; explicit split and bipartite counterexamples on 317,440 vertices; asymptotic many-peak and mode-average constructions; minimum-degree thresholds for unimodality and for a central mode.
